title: Electron-pair sharing reactions
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Chemistry (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-30-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: R3.4#c07 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R3.4#c08 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R3.4#c02 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R3.4#c05 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Electrophile
items.clue: Accepts a pair from its partner to form a new covalent bond.

items.label: Electrophilic addition
items.clue: The typical reaction of alkenes: a species attracted to the C=C joins across it.

items.label: Nucleophilic substitution
items.clue: One group replaces another on a carbon atom as a new bond forms and an old one breaks.

items.label: Homolytic fission
items.clue: Breaking of a covalent bond in which each fragment keeps one of the two bonding electrons, forming two radicals (e.g. Br–Br → 2Br•, as in radical substitution under UV light).

questions.stem:
Ethene reacts with bromine:
CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br
Which reactant acts as the electrophile?

options.text: Br₂, as it accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond
Ethene, as its C=C bond is rich in electrons
Neither, as neither reactant carries a positive charge
Ethene, as its C atoms need electrons for an octet

questions.explanation: Br₂ accepts the electron pair donated by the electron-rich C=C bond, forming a C–Br bond. A neutral molecule can be an electrophile.

questions.stem: Why are alkenes susceptible to attack by electrophiles?

options.text: The C=C double bond is weaker than a C–C single bond.
The C=C double bond is a region of high electron density.
The carbon atoms of C=C are deficient in electrons.
The C=C carbon atoms need more electrons for an octet.

questions.explanation: The double bond concentrates electron density between and around the two carbon atoms, and this electron-rich region attracts electron-pair acceptors.

questions.stem:
Ammonia reacts with hydrogen ions:
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
Which species acts as the electrophile?

options.text: NH₃, as its nitrogen atom carries a lone pair of electrons
Neither, as N and H each supply one electron to the bond
H⁺, as it accepts the lone pair on the nitrogen atom
H⁺, as it forms an ionic bond with the nitrogen atom of NH₃

questions.explanation: H⁺ has no electrons and accepts the lone pair of nitrogen to form the new N–H bond. A positively charged species that accepts a pair is an electrophile.

questions.stem: Ethene is bubbled through a solution of bromine in an organic solvent at room temperature, in the dark. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bromine loses its colour as CH₂BrCH₂Br forms by addition.
The bromine loses its colour as CH₂=CHBr forms by substitution.
No reaction occurs, as Br₂ has no positive charge.
No reaction occurs, as UV light is needed to split Br₂.

questions.explanation: Br₂ adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. The orange-brown colour of bromine disappears; this is the test for C=C.

questions.stem: But-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, undergoes hydration when heated with steam in the presence of an acid catalyst. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Water adds across the C=C bond, forming butane-2,3-diol.
An OH group replaces an H atom, forming but-2-en-2-ol.
H atoms from water add across C=C, forming butane.
Water adds across the C=C bond, forming butan-2-ol.

questions.explanation: H adds to one carbon of C=C and OH to the other: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ + H₂O → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, butan-2-ol.

questions.stem: Ethene is mixed with hydrogen bromide gas at room temperature. Which statement is correct?

options.text: HBr adds across the C=C bond, forming CH₂BrCH₂Br.
A Br atom replaces one H atom, forming CH₂=CHBr.
HBr adds across the C=C bond, forming CH₃CH₂Br.
No reaction occurs, as the HBr molecule is neutral.

questions.explanation: H adds to one carbon and Br to the other: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br, bromoethane.

questions.stem:
Aluminium chloride reacts with chloride ions:
AlCl₃ + Cl⁻ → AlCl₄⁻
Which statement identifies the Lewis acid in this reaction?

options.text: Cl⁻, as it donates an electron pair to AlCl₃
AlCl₃, as it accepts an electron pair from Cl⁻
Neither, as no H⁺ ion is transferred at all
AlCl₃, as Al forms an ionic bond with Cl⁻

questions.explanation: Al in AlCl₃ has only six outer electrons and accepts a lone pair from Cl⁻, forming a coordination bond in AlCl₄⁻. An electron-pair acceptor is a Lewis acid.

questions.stem: Ammonia reacts with boron trifluoride to form H₃NBF₃. The Lewis formula of the product is often drawn with a positive formal charge on N and a negative formal charge on B. Which statement about the new N–B bond is correct?

options.text: It is a coordination bond; both electrons came from N
It is a coordination bond; both of its electrons came from B
It is a covalent bond; N and B each gave an electron
It is an ionic bond, as N carries + and B carries −

questions.explanation: N in NH₃ has a lone pair and B in BF₃ has only six outer electrons. N donates its lone pair to B, forming a coordination bond; the formal charges record this donation.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the bonding between H₂O and Cu²⁺ in the complex ion [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺?

options.text: Cu²⁺ donates an electron pair to each H₂O, forming a coordination bond.
Each H₂O donates a lone pair to Cu²⁺, forming a coordination bond.
Each H₂O is held to Cu²⁺ by an ionic bond, as Cu is a metal.
Each H₂O and the Cu²⁺ give one electron to form a covalent bond.

questions.explanation: Each water ligand donates a lone pair from its oxygen atom to Cu²⁺. Six coordination bonds form, and the ligands act as Lewis bases.

questions.stem: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions by the SN1 mechanism. Which describes the first step?

options.text: The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, forming (CH₃)₃C⁺ and Br⁻.
OH⁻ attacks the C atom as the C–Br bond breaks, in a single step.
The C–Br bond breaks homolytically, giving radicals (CH₃)₃C• and Br•.
The C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, forming (CH₃)₃C⁻ and Br⁺ ions.

questions.explanation: The slow first step of SN1 is heterolysis of C–Br: Br takes the bonding pair (curly arrow from the C–Br bond to Br), giving a tertiary carbocation and Br⁻. OH⁻ attacks the carbocation in the second, fast step.

questions.stem: 1-chloropropane, 1-bromopropane and 1-iodopropane are each warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide under identical conditions. Which reacts fastest, and why?

options.text: 1-chloropropane, as its C–Cl bond is the most polar
1-iodopropane, as its C–I bond is the weakest
1-chloropropane, as the small Cl blocks attack least
None; all react equally fast, as OH⁻ attacks C

questions.explanation: The C–X bond must break for substitution to occur. Bond enthalpy falls from C–Cl to C–Br to C–I, so C–I breaks most easily and 1-iodopropane reacts fastest.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with hydrogen bromide by electrophilic addition. Which describes the curly arrows in the first step of the mechanism?

options.text: From the H atom of HBr to the C=C bond, and from Br to the H–Br bond
From the C=C bond to the Br of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to the H
From the C=C bond to the H of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to Br
Fish-hook arrows split H–Br into H• and Br•, which add to C=C

questions.explanation: The electron-rich C=C bond donates a pair to the δ+ H atom, forming a C–H bond, while the H–Br bonding pair moves onto Br. This gives CH₃CH₂⁺ and Br⁻; Br⁻ then bonds to the carbocation.
